title: Senior's toolkit: setting up EF Core and seeing its SQL
summary: The packages, the dotnet-ef tool and the logging switches you use on day one of any EF Core project.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: setting up EF Core and seeing its SQL
steps.body: Every EF Core project starts with the same few packages and the same habit: look at the SQL it sends. These are the commands and options experienced developers set up first.

toolkit.what: Add the provider for your database. The provider pulls in EF Core itself. Pick one per database: `.SqlServer`, `.Sqlite`, or `Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL`.
flags: also add this to the startup project, or `dotnet ef` cannot run against it
keep every EF package on the same version
toolkit.example:
dotnet add package Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite
dotnet add package Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design

toolkit.what: Install the `dotnet ef` command, which creates migrations and inspects your context. Teams often pin it per repository as a local tool instead.
flags: install for your user, available everywhere
upgrade it to match your EF packages
then `dotnet tool install dotnet-ef` pins the version in the repo
toolkit.example:
dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef
dotnet ef --version
toolkit.when: once per machine, or once per repo with a tool manifest

toolkit.what: Register the context with dependency injection in ASP.NET Core. Each request gets its own scoped instance, and the connection string comes from configuration, not from code.
flags: choose the provider and connection string

toolkit.what: Print what EF Core does, including every SQL command it runs. The fastest way to find out why a query is slow or wrong.
flags: shows executed commands; `Debug` shows much more
only the SQL category, without the noise

toolkit.what: Show parameter values in logs and exception messages instead of `?`. Development only: it writes user data into your logs.
flags: clearer errors when a column value cannot be read into a property
the guard you wrap both in

toolkit.what: Get the SQL for a LINQ query without running it. Paste it into a database client or a code review comment.
flags: works before `ToList()`; it never touches the database
toolkit.example:
var q = db.Books.Where(b => b.Year > 2000).OrderBy(b => b.Title);
Console.WriteLine(q.ToQueryString());
toolkit.when: reviewing what a query will send

steps.prompt: Match each piece to the job it does.
pairs: the provider that talks to the database
lets `dotnet ef` load your startup project
shows the SQL of a query without running it

steps.prompt: You run `dotnet ef migrations add Initial` and get this. What do you do?
code: Your startup project 'Shop.Api' doesn't reference Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design.
This package is required for the Entity Framework Core Tools to work.
options: `dotnet add src/Shop.Api package Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design`, using the same version as your other EF packages
steps.explain: The tool builds and loads your startup project, and it needs the Design package there to do it. The tool itself is installed fine. Keep all EF package versions equal, or you get odd missing-method errors.

steps.prompt: Log only the SQL commands, and show parameter values only in development.
steps.explain: Executed commands are logged at Information. Sensitive data logging puts parameter values (emails, names) into logs, so it stays behind a development check.

steps.prompt: A production log shows `Failed executing DbCommand ... WHERE "u"."Email" = @p0` and you need to know which email failed. A teammate suggests turning on `EnableSensitiveDataLogging()` in production. What is the better answer?
options: Reproduce it locally or in a test environment with sensitive logging on; in production, log the user id yourself instead of raw parameter values
Turn it on in production; logs are private
Switch to `LogLevel.Trace` in production, which shows values safely
Parameter values can never be seen, so give up
steps.explain: Production logs are copied to many systems and kept a long time. Parameter values are user data. Keep the switch for development and add your own non-sensitive context (an id, not an email) to production logs.

items: A local SQLite file as the database
steps.explain: Detailed errors cost a little performance and sensitive logging leaks data, so both stay in development. Logging commands is useful everywhere, routed through your normal logging.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: On every new project, add the provider and Design packages at one version and turn on command logging in development. Whenever a query surprises you, call `ToQueryString()` or read the log before changing the LINQ: the SQL tells you what really happened.
